fields.Name: Sales: Forecast History
fields.UserQuestion: What did we think the forecast was on a past date, and how has it moved since?
fields.Description: Point-in-time forecast from ForecastSnapshot (master plan §9.4). A DIFFERENT QUESTION from "Sales: Forecast by Category", not a variant of it: reconstructing a past forecast from Deal is impossible, not merely inaccurate, because amounts change, dates move and deals get recategorised without the current row carrying what it used to say. CommitChangeSincePrior is the column a forecast review actually reads — not the level, but the movement.
fields.TechnicalDescription: Grain: ForecastSnapshot, written by the Sales.CaptureForecastSnapshot Action on the Sales - Forecast Snapshot (daily) ScheduledJob. (scripts/capture-forecast-snapshot.sql is a manual tool, deliberately unseeded -- see its header.) Two independent date concepts: CapturedAt is when the picture was taken ("as we saw it on the 1st"), PeriodStart/PeriodEnd describe which period it was ABOUT — filtered separately because conflating them answers neither question. Column names are *Amount-suffixed, diverging from §9.5's bare Commit/BestCase/Pipeline/Closed; the shipped names are authoritative per docs/DECISIONS.md D6, since COMMIT is reserved in T-SQL and Postgres and production is Postgres.

_comments: PARAMETERS ARE DERIVED BY MJ, NOT DECLARED HERE -- and the authored detail is kept below.
They were declared as relatedEntities['MJ: Query Parameters'], and that made this whole
directory unseedable on a fresh database. MJ derives parameters from the SQL when the query is
created; the declared rows then collided with them on the UNIQUE (QueryID, Name) index -- 18
violations, whole-transaction rollback, 0 of 16 queries landing, byte-identical on a retry.
That was KI-25, and it cost every fresh install its dashboard.
Removing the declarations lets MJ derive them: names and IsRequired come out identical. Type
degrades from date to string on the period parameters, which is harmless here because
QueryForecastSource passes them as ISO date-only STRINGS on purpose -- 'a full timestamp would
invite a query to compare a date column against an instant'. What would genuinely have been
lost is the authored Description and SampleValue, so they are preserved verbatim:
CompanyID (string)
Selling company. Omit for every company. Deal.CompanyID is server-stamped from the pipeline, so it is always present and never needs a fallback.
PipelineID (string)
One pipeline. Omit for all pipelines.
PeriodStart (date)
Inclusive start of the window. Omit for no lower bound.
PeriodEnd (date)
Inclusive end of the window. Omit for no upper bound.
CapturedOnOrBefore (date)
Show the forecast as it stood on or before this timestamp. This is the "as we saw it then" filter, distinct from the period filters.
